analysis.one_liner: Bars banks from forcing customers into arbitration over credit cards or accounts opened without their consent.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on December 1, 2016, and died there when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After Wells Fargo employees opened millions of bank and credit card accounts customers never asked for, the bank argued those same customers had signed away their right to sue in court because of arbitration clauses in their legitimate accounts. This bill would have said that for any credit card or bank account a customer did not request, a bank's forced-arbitration clause cannot be enforced, so fraud victims could take the bank to court. The bill was sent to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers victimized by unauthorized bank or credit card accounts would gain the right to sue in court instead of being forced into private arbitration, where proceedings are secret, there is no appeal, and class actions are typically barred. The bill's findings tie this directly to the Wells Fargo scandal, where roughly 1.5 million unauthorized accounts were opened and the bank successfully used arbitration clauses to keep victims out of court.

how_it_helps.text: It would bar banks from enforcing forced-arbitration clauses in disputes over credit cards and bank accounts that customers never asked for, letting victims sue in court instead.

The bill's findings describe Wells Fargo using arbitration clauses to force customers into arbitration even over accounts Wells Fargo employees opened without their consent, and cite the case Jabbari v. Wells Fargo, where the bank successfully claimed customers had signed away their court rights.
Its findings state that consumers have no meaningful choice about arbitration and typically do not know they have given up their right to sue.

analysis.who_pays: Banks and credit card issuers would lose the ability to route fraud disputes over unauthorized accounts into arbitration, and would face public lawsuits, class actions, and damages they could otherwise avoid.

drawbacks.text: The ban is narrower than it may appear: it covers only accounts the consumer did not request. For ordinary accounts customers opened themselves, banks could keep using arbitration clauses, and the bill leaves those agreements fully enforceable.

A good-faith objection: arbitration can be faster and cheaper for consumers with small-dollar claims than litigation, and broad bans on arbitration can raise costs for banks that some argue get passed to customers through fees.

A similar CFPB rule restricting forced arbitration in financial contracts was later voided by Congress under the Congressional Review Act in 2017, showing that restrictions on financial-industry arbitration faced strong congressional opposition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers—regaining the right to sue banks that commit fraud against them—outweighs the limited cost to banks of litigating cases they might have forced into private arbitration. The main drawback is that the protection is tied to accounts the customer never requested, so arbitration clauses would survive for ordinary accounts; and arbitration does offer some consumers faster, cheaper resolution for small claims. But for fraud claims—exactly the kind of case the bill's findings show customers losing the ability to pursue—the court access restored is the more valuable safeguard.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or a vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 1, 2016, by Senator Sherrod Brown with 15 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents.
On the same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs—the only action the bill ever received.
The committee took no further action; the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill expired without a markup, a floor vote, or companion action in the House.

The bill was written in response to the Wells Fargo fake-accounts scandal, in which regulators found the bank opened roughly 1.5 million unauthorized checking accounts and 565,000 credit cards, and then argued in court that victims were bound to arbitration.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and credit card issuers kept their ability to force customers into arbitration, including over accounts opened without customer consent. Consumers defrauded through such accounts remain stuck outside the courts.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy, Al Franken, Dick Durbin, and 12 other Democratic and independent senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Banking Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: The bill's referral ended the legislative process; the committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and no action followed before the Congress expired.

against.name: Financial services industry
against.what_they_did: The banking industry generally opposes restrictions on forced arbitration in consumer financial contracts and lobbies against such measures.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republicans supported the bill, and it died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill would strip banks of the ability to enforce arbitration clauses in disputes over unauthorized accounts, exposing them to class actions and individual lawsuits in court over exactly the conduct—like the Wells Fargo fake-accounts scandal—that arbitration clauses otherwise shield from public courtrooms.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and the dispute-resolution industry
industries.note: The bill narrows but does not abolish consumer arbitration; for accounts customers opened themselves, the existing arbitration system continues unchanged.
